title: Profit and Cash Flow
summary: A profitable company can run short of cash. Follow a sale through earnings, investment, and financing to see why.
body_markdown:
A company can report a profit while using cash. It can also generate cash by borrowing, selling assets, or delaying payments, without improving its underlying business. Financial statements help separate those possibilities.


Read them as connected accounts of the same company. The income statement describes revenue and expenses over a period. The balance sheet shows assets, obligations, and owners’ equity at a point in time. The cash-flow statement explains how cash changed. The[SEC’s introductory guide](https://www.sec.gov/investor/pubs/begfinstmtguide.htm) provides the basic map; the useful work is tracing how the statements reconcile.


## A sale before the cash arrives


Consider a simplified company with $100 of recognized sales. Customers have paid $80, leaving $20 to collect. It pays $60 of operating costs and records $10 of depreciation, an accounting charge allocating earlier equipment spending across its useful life. Ignore taxes, interest, and other items for this example.


Reported profit is $100 − $60 − $10 = $30. Operating cash flow is only $80 − $60 = $20. Starting from profit gives the same answer: add back the $10 noncash depreciation, then subtract the $20 increase in unpaid customer bills.


Neither figure is inherently wrong. Profit attempts to match revenue with the costs of earning it. Cash flow reflects when money actually arrives and leaves. A widening gap between them calls for an explanation: perhaps normal growth requires more customer credit, or perhaps collection is deteriorating.


## Growth can consume capital


Suppose the company also spends $35 on equipment. Operating cash flow less that investment is negative $15. The business is profitable on the income statement but needs existing cash or new financing to fund the period’s activity.


The interpretation depends on what the equipment does. Replacing worn-out assets is necessary to sustain current operations. Building profitable new capacity may create future value. Labeling both “investment” does not make both equally productive, and cutting both can improve today’s cash flow while weakening tomorrow’s business.


Working capital creates a similar issue. If sales expand, inventory and unpaid invoices may grow before cash is collected. Supplier credit can offset part of that need. Compare collection, inventory, and payment patterns over several periods and against the company’s actual business model. A retailer paid immediately by customers differs from a supplier offering long payment terms.


## Financing the shortfall


The balance sheet shows whether a company has room to absorb those timing differences. Cash, receivables, inventory, debt, and other obligations help explain its next funding need. An asset can have accounting value without being readily available to pay a bill.


Borrowing $25 would cover the example’s $15 cash shortfall and increase cash by $10. It would not turn the operating result into $45 of cash generation. The cash-flow statement separates financing from operations for this reason.


New equity can also finance growth. That improves the company’s cash position while dividing the ownership among more shares. Evaluate results per share as well as for the company as a whole: a business can become larger without each existing share gaining the same percentage claim on its earnings.


## Adjusted earnings and free cash flow


Management may show adjusted earnings or free cash flow to explain operations. These can be useful, provided the adjustments are understood and consistently applied. Removing a recurring cost because it is inconvenient does not make the economic cost disappear.


The[SEC’s non-GAAP guidance](https://www.sec.gov/rules-regulations/staff-guidance/corporation-finance-interpretations/non-gaap-financial-measures) notes that free cash flow has no uniform definition. Operating cash flow less capital spending is common, but that result need not be available for discretionary use: debt repayment and other commitments may remain.


Revenue growth is only the beginning of the valuation argument. How much becomes profit, how much of that profit arrives as cash, and how much must go back into the business? The amount left for lenders and owners can look quite different from the growth rate in the headline.
